systemsMapSummary: 1:1s are the first thing to fall out of a busy week, and three reinforcing loops explain why. First, a priority loop: nothing protects the slot, so a 1:1 loses every collision with delivery work and gets bumped 'just this once' — which makes it easier to bump next time. Second, a visibility loop: no one can see who is actually holding 1:1s, so there is no accountability and no positive norm — managers who skip pay no cost and managers who hold them get no signal that it matters. Third, a skill loop: managers who were never coached on how to run a 1:1 find them awkward, don't know what to cover, and quietly let them lapse. These compound — an unprotected slot, held by an unsure manager, that no one is watching, reliably disappears. The highest-leverage moment is the calendar itself: a protected, recurring slot that a busy week can't quietly delete.

topLeveragePoints.point: Protect the 1:1 as a recurring, hard-to-move calendar hold
topLeveragePoints.currentState: 1:1s sit in an already-full calendar with nothing defending the slot, so they lose every collision with delivery work.

topLeveragePoints.point: Make holding 1:1s visible to managers and their leaders
topLeveragePoints.currentState: No one can see who is actually holding 1:1s, so there is no accountability and no norm.

topLeveragePoints.point: Give managers a simple, reusable 1:1 structure so it feels easy to run
topLeveragePoints.currentState: Managers who were never coached on 1:1s are unsure what to cover, so the meeting feels awkward and gets dropped.

headline: If we protected the slot, made cadence visible, and gave managers a simple structure to run, we'd likely see 1:1 coverage move from 38% toward the 80% target without adding a new tool.
